passage:
Indu sat her doll on the sofa arm and whispered the game to it. "You are sick. I listen to your chest. Then I give medicine." She tapped the doll's chest twice, then held out an empty spoon.

Later, on the mat, Indu and Uday settled roles: Indu the doctor, Uday the parent. They fetched a toy stethoscope, a bandage and a rug for the clinic before anyone said a word of the story.

At the other end of the room, Varun was playing shop with Tara. "No, you say 'how much?' first," Varun said. "No, not like that." After the fifth correction Tara put the basket down and wandered off to the book corner.

Back at the clinic, the game slowed after the check-up. Uday yawned and looked at the ceiling. Indu jumped up. "Emergency! The baby has a fever!" Uday dashed for the doll, and the clinic was busy again.

qa.q: What did Indu say to the doll?
qa.a: She said, "You are sick. I listen to your chest. Then I give medicine."

qa.q: Why did Indu and Uday's game last while Varun and Tara's ended?
qa.a: Indu and Uday settled roles, fetched a stethoscope and bandage, and Indu shouted about an emergency when the game slowed, while Varun kept saying no to Tara until Tara wandered off after the fifth correction.

qa.q: What was Tara probably feeling after the fifth correction?
qa.a: Fed up and bored, because the game no longer felt like Tara's.
Varun could let Tara make up some lines of Tara's own and add a twist, so the game can go new ways.

grounding: Four approaches to planning a pretend game: talking it through beforehand, setting up roles and props, holding to rigid rules, and adding a problem to the story.
